docs.text: Run the Playbooks # Overview # This document describes the typical execution flow for provisioning and for day-2 compute-node operations. The standard cluster creation flow remains: Run playbooks/0_setup.yaml Run playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml if new LPARs are required Run playbooks/2_create_kvm_host.yaml if new KVM hosts are required Run playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml Run playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml Run playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml Run playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml Run playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml Standard cluster creation flow # 1. Initial setup # Run playbooks/0_setup.yaml first. This playbook: - validates the inventory input - installs required controller dependencies - generates inventories/default/hosts - adds eligible day-2 hypervisors to the day2_hosts section when day2_compute_node is defined and the referenced host_vars files have setup_host: true Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/0_setup.yaml If no eligible day-2 hypervisors are defined, the day2_hosts section is omitted. 2. Create LPARs if needed # If your KVM hosts must be created first, run playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml 3. Create KVM hosts if needed # 0 Setup Playbook # Overview # First-time setup of the Ansible Controller, the machine running Ansible. Outcomes # Packages and Ansible Galaxy collections are confirmed to be installed properly. host_vars files are confirmed to match KVM host(s) hostnames. Ansible inventory is templated out and working properly. SSH key generated for Ansible passwordless authentication. SSH agent is setup on the Ansible Controller. Ansible SSH key is copied to the file server. Notes # You can use an existing SSH key as your Ansible key, or have Ansible create one for you. It is highly recommended to use one without a passphrase. 1 Create LPAR Playbook # Overview # Creation of one to three Logical Partitions (LPARs), depending on your configuration. Uses the Hardware Management Console (HMC) API, so your system must be in Dynamic Partition Manager (DPM) mode. Outcomes # One to three LPARs created. One to two Networking Interface Cards (NICs) attached per LPAR. One to two storage groups attached per LPAR. LPARs are in 'Stopped' state. Notes # Recommend opening the HMC via web-browser to watch the LPARs come up. 2 Create KVM Host Playbook # Overview # First-time start-up of Red Hat Enterprise Linux installed natively on the LPAR(s). Uses the Hardware Management Console (HMC) API, so your system must be in Dynamic Partition Manager (DPM) mode. Configuration files are passed to the file server and RHEL is booted and then kickstarted for fully automated setup. Outcomes # LPAR(s) started up in 'Active' state. Configuration files (cfg, ins, prm) for the KVM host(s) are on the file server in the provided configs directory. Notes # Recommended to open the HMC via web-browser to watch the Operating System Messages for each LPAR as they boot in order to debug any potential problems. 3 Setup KVM Host Playbook # Overview # Configures the RHEL server(s) installed natively on the LPAR(s) to act as virtualization hypervisor(s) to host the virtual machines that make up the eventual cluster. Outcomes # Ansible SSH key is copied to all KVM hosts for passwordless authentication. RHEL subscription is auto-attached to all KVM hosts. Software packages specified in group_vars/all.yaml have been installed. Cockpit console enabled for Graphical User Interface via web browser. Go to http://kvm-ip-here:9090 to view it. TigerVNC server is configured and enabled for remote desktop administration. Connect with a VNC client at kvm-ip-here:5901 (display :1). Libvirt is started and enabled. Logical volume group that was created during kickstart is extended to fill all available space. A macvtap bridge has been created on the host's networking interface. Notes # If you're using a pre-existing LPAR, take a look at roles/configure_storage/tasks/main.yaml to make sure that the commands that will be run to extend the logical volume will work. Storage configurations can vary widely. The values there are the defaults from using autopart during kickstart. Also be aware that if lpar.storage_group_2.auto_config is True, the role roles/configure_storage/tasks/main.yaml will be non-idempotent. Meaning, it will fail if you run it twice. 4 Create Bastion Playbook # Overview # Creates the bastion KVM guest on the first KVM host. The bastion hosts essential services for the cluster. If you already have a bastion server, that can be used instead of running this playbook. Outcomes # Bastion configs are templated out to the file server. Bastion is booted using virt-install. Bastion is kickstarted for fully automated setup of the operating system. Notes # This can be a particularly sticky part of the process. If any of the variables used in the virt-install or kickstart are off, the bastion won't be able to boot. Recommend watching it come up from the first KVM host's cockpit. Go to http://kvm-ip-here:9090 via web-browser to view it. You'll have to sign in, enable administrative access (top right), and then click on the virtual machines tab on the left-hand toolbar. 5 Setup Bastion Playbook # Overview # Configuration of the bastion to host essential infrastructure services for the cluster. Can be first-time setup or use an existing server. Outcomes # Ansible SSH key copied to bastion for passwordless authentication. Software packages specified in group_vars/all.yaml have been installed. An OCP-specific SSH key is generated for passing into the install-config (then passed to the nodes). Firewall is configured to permit traffic through the necessary ports. Domain Name Server (DNS) configured to resolve cluster's IP addresses and APIs. Only done if env.bastion.options.dns is true. DNS is checked to make sure all the necessary Fully Qualified Domain Names, including APIs resolve properly. Also ensures outside access is working. High Availability Proxy (HAProxy) load balancer is configured. Only done if env.bastion.options.loadbalancer.on_bastion is true. If the the cluster is to be highly available (meaning spread across more than one LPAR), an OpenVPN server is setup on the bastion to allow for the KVM hosts to communicate between eachother. OpenVPN clients are configured on the KVM hosts. CoreOS roofts is pulled to the bastion if not already there. OCP client and installer are pulled down if not there already. oc, kubectl and openshift-install binaries are installed. OCP install-config is templated and backed up. In disconnected mode, if platform is mirrored (currently only legacy), image content source policy and additionalTrustBundle is also patched. Manfifests are created. OCP install directory found at /root/ocpinst/ is created and populated with necessary files. Ignition files for the bootstrap, control, and compute nodes are transferred to HTTP-accessible directory for booting nodes. Notes # The stickiest part is DNS setup and get_ocp role at the end. 6 Create Nodes Playbook # Overview # OCP cluster's nodes are created and the control plane is bootstrapped. Outcomes # CoreOS initramfs and kernel are pulled down. Control nodes are created and bootstrapped. Bootstrap has been created, done its job connecting the control plane, and is then destroyed. Compute nodes are created, as many as is specified in groups_vars/all.yaml. Infra nodes, if defined in group_vars/all.yaml have been created, but are at this point essentially just compute nodes. Notes # To watch the bootstrap do its job connecting the control plane: first, SSH to the bastion, then change to root (sudo -i), from there SSH to the bootstrap node as user 'core' (e.g. ssh core@bootstrap-ip). Once you're in the bootstrap run 'journalctl -b -f -u release-image.service -u bootkube.service'. Expect many errors as the control planes come up. You're waiting for the message 'bootkube.service complete' If the cluster is highly available, the bootstrap node will be created on the last (usually third) KVM host in the group. Since the bastion is on the first host, this was done to spread out the load. 7 OCP Verification Playbook # Overview # Final steps of waiting for and verifying the OpenShift cluster to complete its installation. Outcomes # Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs) have been approved. All nodes are in ready state. All cluster operators are available. OpenShift installation is verified to be complete. Temporary credentials and URL are printed to allow easy first-time login to the cluster. Notes # These steps may take a long time and the tasks are very repetitive because of that. If your cluster has a very large number of compute nodes or insufficient resources, more rounds of approvals and time may be needed for these tasks. If you made it this far, congratulations! To install a new cluster, copy your inventory directory, change the default in the ansible.cfg, change the variables, and start again. With all the customizations to the playbooks you made along the way still intact. Additional Playbooks # Delete Cluster Nodes Playbook (delete_cluster_nodes.yaml) # Overview # Use this playbook to delete all cluster nodes (bootstrap, control, compute, and infra nodes) from the configured KVM hosts based on your inventories/default/group_vars/all.yaml configuration. This is useful when you need to tear down the cluster nodes while keeping the bastion and infrastructure intact. Usage # To delete all cluster nodes from all configured KVM hosts: ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml To delete nodes from a specific KVM host only, use tags: ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_1 ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_2 ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_3 Outcomes # All cluster nodes (bootstrap, control, compute, and infra) are destroyed and undefined from the configured KVM hosts. Virtual machine storage is removed. A summary message is displayed upon completion. Notes # This playbook does NOT delete: The bastion node Network configurations Storage pools DNS or HAProxy configurations To verify deletion, run virsh list --all on each KVM host. The playbook uses the existing delete_nodes role which safely handles non-existent VMs. If you need to reinstall the cluster after deletion, use the reinstall_cluster.yaml playbook or run playbooks 6 and 7. Create additional compute nodes (create_compute_node.yaml) and delete compute nodes (delete_compute_node.yaml) # Overview # In case you want to add additional compute nodes in a day-2 operation to your cluster or delete existing compute nodes in your cluster, run these playbooks. Currently we support only env.network_mode macvtap for these two playbooks. We recommand to create a new config file for the additional compute node with such parameters: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/2_create_kvm_host.yaml 4. Configure KVM hosts # Run playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml . This playbook configures: - the primary KVM hosts from the main inventory - any eligible day-2 hypervisors listed in day2_hosts Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml 5. Create the bastion # Run playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml 6. Configure the bastion # Run playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml . This playbook configures bastion services such as DNS, HAProxy, HTTPD, and firewall rules. Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml 7. Create cluster nodes # Run playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml 8. Verify the cluster # Run playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml Day-2 compute-node workflow # Day-2 compute nodes are defined through host_vars files referenced by day2_compute_node . Example in inventories/default/group_vars/all.yaml : day2_compute_node: - example-day2-node The referenced file must exist in inventories/default/host_vars , for example: - inventories/default/host_vars/compute-day2.yaml.template - inventories/default/host_vars/example-day2-node.yaml Day-2 preparation flow # If the day-2 node uses a hypervisor that must be prepared, run these playbooks in order: playbooks/0_setup.yaml playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml Why this is required: - playbooks/0_setup.yaml refreshes inventories/default/hosts and rebuilds day2_hosts - playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml configures the hypervisor when setup_host: true - playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml reconciles bastion DNS and HAProxy entries for the day-2 nodes when: - dns: true - loadbalancer.on_bastion: true If a day-2 node is removed from day2_compute_node and playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml is rerun, the bastion reconciliation removes obsolete DNS and HAProxy entries. Create a single day-2 compute node # After the preparation flow is complete, create the node with playbooks/create_compute_node.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/create_compute_node.yaml This playbook: - loads the first entry from day2_compute_node - reads the matching host_vars file - creates the VM on the referenced hypervisor - uses disk_size when defined - otherwise falls back to env.cluster.nodes.compute.disk_size - uses storage.pool_name when defined - otherwise falls back to {{ env.cluster.networking.metadata_name }}-vdisk - uses networking.dhcp: true to boot the day-2 node with DHCP and apply the configured guest MAC address - uses networking.dhcp: false to boot the day-2 node with static network kernel arguments from the host_vars file Create multiple day-2 compute nodes # For multiple nodes, use playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml with an extra-vars file. Example extra-vars file: day2_compute_nodes: - example-day2-node - another-day2-node Run: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml -e @day2-nodes.yaml If those nodes require new hypervisors to be configured first, temporarily add the relevant host_vars entry names to day2_compute_node , rerun: - playbooks/0_setup.yaml - playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml - playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml and then run playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml . Delete a day-2 compute node # To delete a day-2 node, keep the matching host_vars entry available and run playbooks/delete_compute_node.yaml . Reinstall Cluster Playbook (reinstall_cluster.yaml) # Overview # In case the cluster needs to be completely reinstalled, run this playbook. It will refresh the ingitions that expire after 24 hours, teardown the nodes and re-create them, and then verify the installation. Outcomes # get_ocp role runs. Delete the folders /var/www/html/bin and /var/www/html/ignition. CoreOS roofts is pulled to the bastion. OCP client and installer are pulled down. oc, kubectl and openshift-install binaries are installed. OCP install-config is created from scratch, templated and backed up. Manfifests are created. OCP install directory found at /root/ocpinst/ is deleted, re-created and populated with necessary files. Ignition files for the bootstrap, control, and compute nodes are transferred to HTTP-accessible directory for booting nodes. 6 Create Nodes playbook runs, tearing down and recreating cluster nodes. 7 OCP Verification playbook runs, verifying new deployment. Test Playbook (test.yaml) # Overview # Use this playbook for your testing purposes, if needed. Verify OCP Virtualization Prerequisites (playbooks/operators/verify_ocp_virt_prereqs.yaml) # Overview # Read-only pre-flight check that verifies all 14 prerequisites required before running install_ocp_virt.yaml . Runs every check even if earlier ones fail, then prints a consolidated pass/fail/warn summary. Safe to run at any time — it never creates or modifies any cluster resources. Usage # ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/verify_ocp_virt_prereqs.yaml --ask-vault-pass Outcomes # Prints [FAIL] for each hard prerequisite that is not met. Prints [WARN] for advisory conditions (non-s390x architecture, possible guest nodes, low resource headroom). Exits 0 (pass) when all hard checks succeed, even if warnings are present. Exits non-zero when one or more hard checks fail — resolve before installing. Checks performed # # Check Result type 1 kubeconfig present at ocp_virt_kubeconfig FAIL 2 oc binary present on bastion FAIL 3 Cluster API reachable FAIL 4 cluster-admin privileges FAIL 5 OCP version ≥ 4.19 FAIL 6 All cluster operators healthy FAIL 7 All nodes Ready FAIL 8 Node architecture is s390x WARN 9 Nodes are bare-metal LPARs (not z/VM or KVM guests); read from /proc/sysinfo on each node via oc debug WARN 10 redhat-operators CatalogSource is READY FAIL 11 Default StorageClass exists FAIL 12 Sufficient CPU / memory headroom (≥ 16 vCPU / 32 GiB) WARN 13 kubernetes.core collection installed on Ansible controller FAIL 14 ocp_virt variable defined in operators.yaml FAIL ### Notes * operators.yaml must be present (copy from operators.yaml.template ) before running, as check 14 reads variables from it. * Run this playbook first, fix all [FAIL] items, then run install_ocp_virt.yaml . Install OpenShift Virtualization (playbooks/operators/install_ocp_virt.yaml) # Overview # Installs OpenShift Virtualization as a day-2 operator on a running OCP 4.19+ cluster on IBM Z / LinuxONE (s390x). Runs on the bastion after 7_ocp_verification.yaml has completed. Installs Node Feature Discovery, cert-manager, and the OpenShift Virtualization operator in sequence. Creates the HyperConverged CR to activate the full virtualization stack. Usage # Before running, copy the template and configure your variables: cp inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml.template \ inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml # Edit operators.yaml — at minimum set ocp_virt.hyperconverged.default_cpu_model Then run the playbook: ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/install_ocp_virt.yaml --ask-vault-pass Outcomes # NFD Operator installed and node labelling active (CPU model labels on each node). cert-manager Operator installed. OpenShift Virtualization Operator installed in openshift-cnv namespace. HyperConverged CR created — virtualization stack active. virt-operator , virt-controller , virt-handler pods running. virtctl downloaded from the cluster ( ConsoleCLIDownload ) and installed on the bastion in ocp_virt.virtctl.install_dir (default /usr/local/bin ). Skipped if virtctl is already there or ocp_virt.virtctl.install: false . Optional: a test VM is created and verified Running ( ocp_virt.test_vm.create: true ) and either kept or removed again ( ocp_virt.test_vm.keep ). Notes # Requires OCP 4.19 or later (s390x GA release for OpenShift Virtualization). The playbook fails with a clear message on older versions. The cluster must be installed on LPAR nodes. VM scheduling requires hardware virtualisation at the LPAR level. A default StorageClass must exist before running. Storage provisioner setup (ODF, HPP, etc.) is out of scope — complete it first, then run this playbook. The stable channel always resolves to the OCP Virt version matching the cluster. Pin to a specific release with ocp_virt.channel: stable-4.22 . The test VM requires an s390x qcow2 guest image (e.g. RHEL 9 KVM Guest Image for s390x) reachable over HTTP(S) from the cluster nodes, for example hosted on the bastion file server. The playbook only checks reachability from the bastion and prints a warning if that fails; CDI downloads the image from the cluster network, so a failed import is reported by the failure diagnostics instead. Copy operators.yaml.template to operators.yaml and configure ocp_virt: variables before running (see inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml.template ). virtctl installation (task file roles/install_ocp_virt_operator/tasks/install_virtctl.yaml ) runs after the HyperConverged CR is Available and before the optional test VM: The Linux download link matching the bastion's architecture ( uname -m : x86_64, aarch64/arm64, s390x, ppc64le) is read from the ConsoleCLIDownload object virtctl-clidownloads-kubevirt-hyperconverged , downloaded, extracted and copied to <install_dir>/virtctl . The installed client version is printed. The bastion must be able to reach the cluster's download route over HTTPS, must have tar (GNU) or unzip to unpack the archive, and the playbook user must be allowed to write to install_dir (default /usr/local/bin , normally root ). The playbook fails with a clear message if the cluster offers no virtctl for the bastion's architecture. Set ocp_virt.virtctl.install: false and install it manually in that case. An existing <install_dir>/virtctl is never overwritten. To upgrade, delete the old binary and re-run the playbook. Variable Default Description ocp_virt.virtctl.install true false skips the download and installation. ocp_virt.virtctl.install_dir /usr/local/bin Directory the binary is installed into. ocp_virt.virtctl.validate_certs false Validate the TLS certificate of the download route (it is signed by the cluster's own CA). Create OCP Virt Test VM (playbooks/operators/create_test_vm.yaml) # Overview # Creates a test VirtualMachine on an already-running OCP Virt cluster. Use this when install_ocp_virt.yaml was run with test_vm.create: false and you want to verify the full stack (CDI image import → VM boot) without re-running the operator install. Optionally, the playbook also attaches a blank data disk to the VM ( test_vm.data_disk.create: true ) and triggers a live migration of the VM to another node ( test_vm.migration.enabled: true ). The purpose of this use case is to verify the functionality of OpenShift Virtualization and the underlying storage provider : the storage provider must dynamically provision the root and data disks, and, because live migration requires the disks to be accessible from both the source and the target node, it must support shared ReadWriteMany volumes. Requirements # OCP Virt ( kubevirt-hyperconverged ) already installed and HyperConverged Available ocp_virt.test_vm.image_url set to an s390x qcow2 HTTP(S) URL in operators.yaml Default StorageClass present (CDI needs it for the DataVolume), or ocp_virt.test_vm.storage_class set For the migration test: at least two schedulable worker nodes with enough free memory for a second virt-launcher pod, and a StorageClass that supports ReadWriteMany Usage # ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/create_test_vm.yaml --ask-vault-pass Relevant settings in operators.yaml : ocp_virt: test_vm: keep: true # keep the VM so it can be inspected after the test storage_class: "<rwx-capable-storageclass>" data_disk: create: true # blank data disk, attached as a second virtio disk size: 10Gi storage_class: "" # empty = same as root disk migration: enabled: true # live-migrate the VM after it is Ready timeout: 600 # seconds to wait for the migration to finish Outcomes # Creates the VM namespace and VirtualMachine resource Waits for the DataVolume import to finish (up to dv_timeout seconds) If data_disk.create: true : creates a blank DataVolume <name>-data , attaches it to the VM (serial datadisk , visible in the guest as /dev/disk/by-id/virtio-datadisk ) and waits for it to be ready. The disk is unformatted; partition and mount it inside the guest. Waits for the VM to reach Ready (up to vm_timeout seconds) If migration.enabled: true , after the VM is Ready the playbook: Requests the VM disks with access mode ReadWriteMany Checks the LiveMigratable condition of the VMI (fails with the reason if False ) Creates a VirtualMachineInstanceMigration ( <name>-migration ) Waits for the migration phase Succeeded (up to migration.timeout seconds) Verifies the VMI is Running , migrationState.completed is true, the migration did not fail, and the VM now runs on a different node than before Waits for the VM to be Ready again; on failure it prints oc describe vmim Prints the VMI phase, node name, IP address, data disk PVC status and the migration result ( <source node> -> <target node> ) Deletes the namespace when test_vm.keep: false (default — smoke test behaviour) Leaves the VM and namespace in place when test_vm.keep: true Notes # test_vm.ssh_public_key left empty → bastion's ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub is injected automatically The playbook verifies HyperConverged is Available before creating the VM A migration failure usually means the storage class cannot provide ReadWriteMany volumes (VMI condition LiveMigratable is False ), or no other node can host the VM. Check the StorageProfile of the class: oc get storageprofile <class> -o yaml . To manually verify data integrity across the migration, format and mount the data disk in the guest and write a file before the test; it is still readable afterwards. Manual migration of a kept VM: virtctl migrate <vm> -n <namespace> Failure diagnostics: if any step of the test VM flow fails or times out (DataVolume import, VM start, migration), the playbook prints the cluster state before it fails: the VM, DataVolume, PVC and pod list, oc describe dv , the namespace events (warnings first), the pod waiting reasons and the storage class. It also adds a hint for common causes ( FailedAttachVolume / FailedMount = storage CSI driver cannot attach or mount the volume, ProvisioningFailed , ErrImagePull , FailedScheduling , ImportFailed ). With test_vm.keep: false the namespace is deleted afterwards; set keep: true to leave the stuck resources in place for further debugging. How to log in to the test VM # The VM is only available after the run when test_vm.keep: true . When keep: true , the playbook prints the exact login commands at the end of the run. The VM is created for user cloud-user with the bastion's public key injected through cloud-init (no password is set). The VM sits on the pod network (masquerade), so its IP is a pod IP that the bastion cannot normally reach directly; log in with virtctl instead. On the bastion: export KUBECONFIG=<ocp_virt_kubeconfig> oc get vmi ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test # VM must be Running # SSH with the private key matching the injected public key virtctl ssh cloud-user@vmi/ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # Serial console (exit with Ctrl+]); needs a password, so SSH is preferred virtctl console ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test Replace ocp-virt-test with test_vm.name / test_vm.namespace if you changed them. install_ocp_virt.yaml installs virtctl on the bastion ( ocp_virt.virtctl.install: true ). If it is missing (for example when install_ocp_virt.yaml was run with virtctl.install: false ), download it from the cluster: oc get consoleclidownload virtctl-clidownloads-kubevirt-hyperconverged -o jsonpath='{.spec.links[*].href}' Without virtctl , SSH through the node running the VM: ssh -J core@<node> cloud-user@<vmi-ip> (node and IP from oc get vmi <vm> -n <ns> -o wide ). If no bastion public key was found and test_vm.ssh_public_key was empty, key login is not possible. Set test_vm.ssh_public_key and recreate the VM. Inside the guest, the data disk is available as /dev/disk/by-id/virtio-datadisk . Uninstall OpenShift Virtualization (playbooks/operators/uninstall_ocp_virt.yaml) # Overview # Removes OpenShift Virtualization, cert-manager, and NFD from the cluster in reverse installation order. Follows the OCP 4.22 uninstall procedure. All VirtualMachine and VirtualMachineInstance objects must be deleted before running — the playbook aborts with a clear message if any remain. Usage # ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/uninstall_ocp_virt.yaml \ -e ocp_virt_uninstall_confirm=true --ask-vault-pass Outcomes # HyperConverged CR deleted — virtualization stack deactivated. OpenShift Virtualization Operator, CSV, and CRDs removed. openshift-cnv namespace deleted. cert-manager Operator, CSV, and the cert-manager-operator and cert-manager namespaces deleted. NFD NodeFeatureDiscovery CR, Operator, CSV, and openshift-nfd namespace deleted. Notes # Requires -e ocp_virt_uninstall_confirm=true — the play aborts immediately without this flag to prevent accidental runs. The variable has no default; setting it in operators.yaml or other vars files is not supported — pass it on the command line. Will abort with a clear message if any VMs or VMIs still exist on the cluster. Cluster operators and compute nodes are not affected. StorageClasses, PVCs, and NFD node labels are not removed by this playbook. operators.yaml must still be present (same requirement as the install playbook).
docs.title: 4 Run the Playbooks

docs.text: This document describes the typical execution flow for provisioning and for day-2 compute-node operations. The standard cluster creation flow remains: Run playbooks/0_setup.yaml Run playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml if new LPARs are required Run playbooks/2_create_kvm_host.yaml if new KVM hosts are required Run playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml Run playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml Run playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml Run playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml Run playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Run playbooks/0_setup.yaml first. This playbook: - validates the inventory input - installs required controller dependencies - generates inventories/default/hosts - adds eligible day-2 hypervisors to the day2_hosts section when day2_compute_node is defined and the referenced host_vars files have setup_host: true Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/0_setup.yaml If no eligible day-2 hypervisors are defined, the day2_hosts section is omitted.
docs.title: 1. Initial setup

docs.text: If your KVM hosts must be created first, run playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/1_create_lpar.yaml
docs.title: 2. Create LPARs if needed

docs.text: First-time setup of the Ansible Controller, the machine running Ansible.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Packages and Ansible Galaxy collections are confirmed to be installed properly. host_vars files are confirmed to match KVM host(s) hostnames. Ansible inventory is templated out and working properly. SSH key generated for Ansible passwordless authentication. SSH agent is setup on the Ansible Controller. Ansible SSH key is copied to the file server.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: You can use an existing SSH key as your Ansible key, or have Ansible create one for you. It is highly recommended to use one without a passphrase.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Creation of one to three Logical Partitions (LPARs), depending on your configuration. Uses the Hardware Management Console (HMC) API, so your system must be in Dynamic Partition Manager (DPM) mode.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: One to three LPARs created. One to two Networking Interface Cards (NICs) attached per LPAR. One to two storage groups attached per LPAR. LPARs are in 'Stopped' state.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: Recommend opening the HMC via web-browser to watch the LPARs come up.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: First-time start-up of Red Hat Enterprise Linux installed natively on the LPAR(s). Uses the Hardware Management Console (HMC) API, so your system must be in Dynamic Partition Manager (DPM) mode. Configuration files are passed to the file server and RHEL is booted and then kickstarted for fully automated setup.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: LPAR(s) started up in 'Active' state. Configuration files (cfg, ins, prm) for the KVM host(s) are on the file server in the provided configs directory.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: Recommended to open the HMC via web-browser to watch the Operating System Messages for each LPAR as they boot in order to debug any potential problems.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Configures the RHEL server(s) installed natively on the LPAR(s) to act as virtualization hypervisor(s) to host the virtual machines that make up the eventual cluster.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Ansible SSH key is copied to all KVM hosts for passwordless authentication. RHEL subscription is auto-attached to all KVM hosts. Software packages specified in group_vars/all.yaml have been installed. Cockpit console enabled for Graphical User Interface via web browser. Go to http://kvm-ip-here:9090 to view it. TigerVNC server is configured and enabled for remote desktop administration. Connect with a VNC client at kvm-ip-here:5901 (display :1). Libvirt is started and enabled. Logical volume group that was created during kickstart is extended to fill all available space. A macvtap bridge has been created on the host's networking interface.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: If you're using a pre-existing LPAR, take a look at roles/configure_storage/tasks/main.yaml to make sure that the commands that will be run to extend the logical volume will work. Storage configurations can vary widely. The values there are the defaults from using autopart during kickstart. Also be aware that if lpar.storage_group_2.auto_config is True, the role roles/configure_storage/tasks/main.yaml will be non-idempotent. Meaning, it will fail if you run it twice.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Creates the bastion KVM guest on the first KVM host. The bastion hosts essential services for the cluster. If you already have a bastion server, that can be used instead of running this playbook.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Bastion configs are templated out to the file server. Bastion is booted using virt-install. Bastion is kickstarted for fully automated setup of the operating system.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: This can be a particularly sticky part of the process. If any of the variables used in the virt-install or kickstart are off, the bastion won't be able to boot. Recommend watching it come up from the first KVM host's cockpit. Go to http://kvm-ip-here:9090 via web-browser to view it. You'll have to sign in, enable administrative access (top right), and then click on the virtual machines tab on the left-hand toolbar.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Configuration of the bastion to host essential infrastructure services for the cluster. Can be first-time setup or use an existing server.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Ansible SSH key copied to bastion for passwordless authentication. Software packages specified in group_vars/all.yaml have been installed. An OCP-specific SSH key is generated for passing into the install-config (then passed to the nodes). Firewall is configured to permit traffic through the necessary ports. Domain Name Server (DNS) configured to resolve cluster's IP addresses and APIs. Only done if env.bastion.options.dns is true. DNS is checked to make sure all the necessary Fully Qualified Domain Names, including APIs resolve properly. Also ensures outside access is working. High Availability Proxy (HAProxy) load balancer is configured. Only done if env.bastion.options.loadbalancer.on_bastion is true. If the the cluster is to be highly available (meaning spread across more than one LPAR), an OpenVPN server is setup on the bastion to allow for the KVM hosts to communicate between eachother. OpenVPN clients are configured on the KVM hosts. CoreOS roofts is pulled to the bastion if not already there. OCP client and installer are pulled down if not there already. oc, kubectl and openshift-install binaries are installed. OCP install-config is templated and backed up. In disconnected mode, if platform is mirrored (currently only legacy), image content source policy and additionalTrustBundle is also patched. Manfifests are created. OCP install directory found at /root/ocpinst/ is created and populated with necessary files. Ignition files for the bootstrap, control, and compute nodes are transferred to HTTP-accessible directory for booting nodes.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: The stickiest part is DNS setup and get_ocp role at the end.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: OCP cluster's nodes are created and the control plane is bootstrapped.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: CoreOS initramfs and kernel are pulled down. Control nodes are created and bootstrapped. Bootstrap has been created, done its job connecting the control plane, and is then destroyed. Compute nodes are created, as many as is specified in groups_vars/all.yaml. Infra nodes, if defined in group_vars/all.yaml have been created, but are at this point essentially just compute nodes.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: To watch the bootstrap do its job connecting the control plane: first, SSH to the bastion, then change to root (sudo -i), from there SSH to the bootstrap node as user 'core' (e.g. ssh core@bootstrap-ip). Once you're in the bootstrap run 'journalctl -b -f -u release-image.service -u bootkube.service'. Expect many errors as the control planes come up. You're waiting for the message 'bootkube.service complete' If the cluster is highly available, the bootstrap node will be created on the last (usually third) KVM host in the group. Since the bastion is on the first host, this was done to spread out the load.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Final steps of waiting for and verifying the OpenShift cluster to complete its installation.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs) have been approved. All nodes are in ready state. All cluster operators are available. OpenShift installation is verified to be complete. Temporary credentials and URL are printed to allow easy first-time login to the cluster.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: These steps may take a long time and the tasks are very repetitive because of that. If your cluster has a very large number of compute nodes or insufficient resources, more rounds of approvals and time may be needed for these tasks. If you made it this far, congratulations! To install a new cluster, copy your inventory directory, change the default in the ansible.cfg, change the variables, and start again. With all the customizations to the playbooks you made along the way still intact.
docs.title: Notes

docs.text: Use this playbook to delete all cluster nodes (bootstrap, control, compute, and infra nodes) from the configured KVM hosts based on your inventories/default/group_vars/all.yaml configuration. This is useful when you need to tear down the cluster nodes while keeping the bastion and infrastructure intact.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: To delete all cluster nodes from all configured KVM hosts: ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml To delete nodes from a specific KVM host only, use tags: ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_1 ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_2 ansible-playbook playbooks/delete_cluster_nodes.yaml --tags kvm_host_3
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: All cluster nodes (bootstrap, control, compute, and infra) are destroyed and undefined from the configured KVM hosts. Virtual machine storage is removed. A summary message is displayed upon completion.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: This playbook does NOT delete: The bastion node Network configurations Storage pools DNS or HAProxy configurations To verify deletion, run virsh list --all on each KVM host. The playbook uses the existing delete_nodes role which safely handles non-existent VMs. If you need to reinstall the cluster after deletion, use the reinstall_cluster.yaml playbook or run playbooks 6 and 7.
docs.title: Notes
Create additional compute nodes (create_compute_node.yaml) and delete compute nodes (delete_compute_node.yaml)

docs.text: In case you want to add additional compute nodes in a day-2 operation to your cluster or delete existing compute nodes in your cluster, run these playbooks. Currently we support only env.network_mode macvtap for these two playbooks. We recommand to create a new config file for the additional compute node with such parameters: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/2_create_kvm_host.yaml
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Run playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml . This playbook configures: - the primary KVM hosts from the main inventory - any eligible day-2 hypervisors listed in day2_hosts Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml
docs.title: 4. Configure KVM hosts

docs.text: Run playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/4_create_bastion.yaml
docs.title: 5. Create the bastion

docs.text: Run playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml . This playbook configures bastion services such as DNS, HAProxy, HTTPD, and firewall rules. Example: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml
docs.title: 6. Configure the bastion

docs.text: Run playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/6_create_nodes.yaml
docs.title: 7. Create cluster nodes

docs.text: Run playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/7_ocp_verification.yaml
docs.title: 8. Verify the cluster

docs.text: Day-2 compute nodes are defined through host_vars files referenced by day2_compute_node . Example in inventories/default/group_vars/all.yaml : day2_compute_node: - example-day2-node The referenced file must exist in inventories/default/host_vars , for example: - inventories/default/host_vars/compute-day2.yaml.template - inventories/default/host_vars/example-day2-node.yaml
docs.title: Day-2 compute-node workflow

docs.text: If the day-2 node uses a hypervisor that must be prepared, run these playbooks in order: playbooks/0_setup.yaml playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml Why this is required: - playbooks/0_setup.yaml refreshes inventories/default/hosts and rebuilds day2_hosts - playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml configures the hypervisor when setup_host: true - playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml reconciles bastion DNS and HAProxy entries for the day-2 nodes when: - dns: true - loadbalancer.on_bastion: true If a day-2 node is removed from day2_compute_node and playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml is rerun, the bastion reconciliation removes obsolete DNS and HAProxy entries.
docs.title: Day-2 preparation flow

docs.text: After the preparation flow is complete, create the node with playbooks/create_compute_node.yaml . ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/create_compute_node.yaml This playbook: - loads the first entry from day2_compute_node - reads the matching host_vars file - creates the VM on the referenced hypervisor - uses disk_size when defined - otherwise falls back to env.cluster.nodes.compute.disk_size - uses storage.pool_name when defined - otherwise falls back to {{ env.cluster.networking.metadata_name }}-vdisk - uses networking.dhcp: true to boot the day-2 node with DHCP and apply the configured guest MAC address - uses networking.dhcp: false to boot the day-2 node with static network kernel arguments from the host_vars file
docs.title: Create a single day-2 compute node

docs.text: For multiple nodes, use playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml with an extra-vars file. Example extra-vars file: day2_compute_nodes: - example-day2-node - another-day2-node Run: ansible-playbook -i inventories/default playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml -e @day2-nodes.yaml If those nodes require new hypervisors to be configured first, temporarily add the relevant host_vars entry names to day2_compute_node , rerun: - playbooks/0_setup.yaml - playbooks/3_setup_kvm_host.yaml - playbooks/5_setup_bastion.yaml and then run playbooks/create_multiple_compute_nodes.yaml .
docs.title: Create multiple day-2 compute nodes

docs.text: To delete a day-2 node, keep the matching host_vars entry available and run playbooks/delete_compute_node.yaml .
docs.title: Delete a day-2 compute node

docs.text: In case the cluster needs to be completely reinstalled, run this playbook. It will refresh the ingitions that expire after 24 hours, teardown the nodes and re-create them, and then verify the installation.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: get_ocp role runs. Delete the folders /var/www/html/bin and /var/www/html/ignition. CoreOS roofts is pulled to the bastion. OCP client and installer are pulled down. oc, kubectl and openshift-install binaries are installed. OCP install-config is created from scratch, templated and backed up. Manfifests are created. OCP install directory found at /root/ocpinst/ is deleted, re-created and populated with necessary files. docs.title: Overview

docs.text: Read-only pre-flight check that verifies all 14 prerequisites required before running install_ocp_virt.yaml . Runs every check even if earlier ones fail, then prints a consolidated pass/fail/warn summary. Safe to run at any time — it never creates or modifies any cluster resources.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/verify_ocp_virt_prereqs.yaml --ask-vault-pass
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Prints [FAIL] for each hard prerequisite that is not met. Prints [WARN] for advisory conditions (non-s390x architecture, possible guest nodes, low resource headroom). Exits 0 (pass) when all hard checks succeed, even if warnings are present. Exits non-zero when one or more hard checks fail — resolve before installing.

docs.text: Installs OpenShift Virtualization as a day-2 operator on a running OCP 4.19+ cluster on IBM Z / LinuxONE (s390x). Runs on the bastion after 7_ocp_verification.yaml has completed. Installs Node Feature Discovery, cert-manager, and the OpenShift Virtualization operator in sequence. Creates the HyperConverged CR to activate the full virtualization stack.

docs.text: Before running, copy the template and configure your variables: cp inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml.template \ inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml # Edit operators.yaml — at minimum set ocp_virt.hyperconverged.default_cpu_model Then run the playbook: ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/install_ocp_virt.yaml --ask-vault-pass

docs.text: NFD Operator installed and node labelling active (CPU model labels on each node). cert-manager Operator installed. OpenShift Virtualization Operator installed in openshift-cnv namespace. VM scheduling requires hardware virtualisation at the LPAR level. A default StorageClass must exist before running. Storage provisioner setup (ODF, HPP, etc.) is out of scope — complete it first, then run this playbook. The stable channel always resolves to the OCP Virt version matching the cluster. Pin to a specific release with ocp_virt.channel: stable-4.22 . The test VM requires an s390x qcow2 guest image (e.g. RHEL 9 KVM Guest Image for s390x) reachable over HTTP(S) from the cluster nodes, for example hosted on the bastion file server. The playbook only checks reachability from the bastion and prints a warning if that fails; CDI downloads the image from the cluster network, so a failed import is reported by the failure diagnostics instead. Copy operators.yaml.template to operators.yaml and configure ocp_virt: variables before running (see inventories/default/group_vars/operators.yaml.template ). virtctl installation (task file roles/install_ocp_virt_operator/tasks/install_virtctl.yaml ) runs after the HyperConverged CR is Available and before the optional test VM: The Linux download link matching the bastion's architecture ( uname -m : x86_64, aarch64/arm64, s390x, ppc64le) is read from the ConsoleCLIDownload object virtctl-clidownloads-kubevirt-hyperconverged , downloaded, extracted and copied to <install_dir>/virtctl . The installed client version is printed. The bastion must be able to reach the cluster's download route over HTTPS, must have tar (GNU) or unzip to unpack the archive, and the playbook user must be allowed to write to install_dir (default /usr/local/bin , normally root ). The playbook fails with a clear message if the cluster offers no virtctl for the bastion's architecture. Set ocp_virt.virtctl.install: false and install it manually in that case. An existing <install_dir>/virtctl is never overwritten. To upgrade, delete the old binary and re-run the playbook. Variable Default Description ocp_virt.virtctl.install true false skips the download and installation. ocp_virt.virtctl.install_dir /usr/local/bin Directory the binary is installed into. ocp_virt.virtctl.validate_certs false Validate the TLS certificate of the download route (it is signed by the cluster's own CA).

docs.text: Creates a test VirtualMachine on an already-running OCP Virt cluster. Use this when install_ocp_virt.yaml was run with test_vm.create: false and you want to verify the full stack (CDI image import → VM boot) without re-running the operator install. Optionally, the playbook also attaches a blank data disk to the VM ( test_vm.data_disk.create: true ) and triggers a live migration of the VM to another node ( test_vm.migration.enabled: true ). The purpose of this use case is to verify the functionality of OpenShift Virtualization and the underlying storage provider : the storage provider must dynamically provision the root and data disks, and, because live migration requires the disks to be accessible from both the source and the target node, it must support shared ReadWriteMany volumes.
docs.title: Overview

docs.text: OCP Virt ( kubevirt-hyperconverged ) already installed and HyperConverged Available ocp_virt.test_vm.image_url set to an s390x qcow2 HTTP(S) URL in operators.yaml Default StorageClass present (CDI needs it for the DataVolume), or ocp_virt.test_vm.storage_class set For the migration test: at least two schedulable worker nodes with enough free memory for a second virt-launcher pod, and a StorageClass that supports ReadWriteMany
docs.title: Requirements

docs.text: ansible-playbook playbooks/operators/create_test_vm.yaml --ask-vault-pass Relevant settings in operators.yaml : ocp_virt: test_vm: keep: true # keep the VM so it can be inspected after the test storage_class: "<rwx-capable-storageclass>" data_disk: create: true # blank data disk, attached as a second virtio disk size: 10Gi storage_class: "" # empty = same as root disk migration: enabled: true # live-migrate the VM after it is Ready timeout: 600 # seconds to wait for the migration to finish
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Creates the VM namespace and VirtualMachine resource Waits for the DataVolume import to finish (up to dv_timeout seconds) If data_disk.create: true : creates a blank DataVolume <name>-data , attaches it to the VM (serial datadisk , visible in the guest as /dev/disk/by-id/virtio-datadisk ) and waits for it to be ready. The disk is unformatted; partition and mount it inside the guest. Waits for the VM to reach Ready (up to vm_timeout seconds) If migration.enabled: true , after the VM is Ready the playbook: Requests the VM disks with access mode ReadWriteMany Checks the LiveMigratable condition of the VMI (fails with the reason if False ) Creates a VirtualMachineInstanceMigration ( <name>-migration ) Waits for the migration phase Succeeded (up to migration.timeout seconds) Verifies the VMI is Running , migrationState.completed is true, the migration did not fail, and the VM now runs on a different node than before Waits for the VM to be Ready again; on failure it prints oc describe vmim Prints the VMI phase, node name, IP address, data disk PVC status and the migration result ( <source node> -> <target node> ) Deletes the namespace when test_vm.keep: false (default — smoke test behaviour) Leaves the VM and namespace in place when test_vm.keep: true
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: test_vm.ssh_public_key left empty → bastion's ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub is injected automatically The playbook verifies HyperConverged is Available before creating the VM A migration failure usually means the storage class cannot provide ReadWriteMany volumes (VMI condition LiveMigratable is False ), or no other node can host the VM. Check the StorageProfile of the class: oc get storageprofile <class> -o yaml . To manually verify data integrity across the migration, format and mount the data disk in the guest and write a file before the test; it is still readable afterwards. Manual migration of a kept VM: virtctl migrate <vm> -n <namespace> Failure diagnostics: if any step of the test VM flow fails or times out (DataVolume import, VM start, migration), the playbook prints the cluster state before it fails: the VM, DataVolume, PVC and pod list, oc describe dv , the namespace events (warnings first), the pod waiting reasons and the storage class. It also adds a hint for common causes ( FailedAttachVolume / FailedMount = storage CSI driver cannot attach or mount the volume, ProvisioningFailed , ErrImagePull , FailedScheduling , ImportFailed ). With test_vm.keep: false the namespace is deleted afterwards; set keep: true to leave the stuck resources in place for further debugging.

docs.text: The VM is only available after the run when test_vm.keep: true . When keep: true , the playbook prints the exact login commands at the end of the run. The VM is created for user cloud-user with the bastion's public key injected through cloud-init (no password is set). The VM sits on the pod network (masquerade), so its IP is a pod IP that the bastion cannot normally reach directly; log in with virtctl instead. On the bastion: export KUBECONFIG=<ocp_virt_kubeconfig> oc get vmi ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test # VM must be Running # SSH with the private key matching the injected public key virtctl ssh cloud-user@vmi/ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # Serial console (exit with Ctrl+]); needs a password, so SSH is preferred virtctl console ocp-virt-test -n ocp-virt-test Replace ocp-virt-test with test_vm.name / test_vm.namespace if you changed them. install_ocp_virt.yaml installs virtctl on the bastion ( ocp_virt.virtctl.install: true ). If it is missing (for example when install_ocp_virt.yaml was run with virtctl.install: false ), download it from the cluster: oc get consoleclidownload virtctl-clidownloads-kubevirt-hyperconverged -o jsonpath='{.spec.links[*].href}' Without virtctl , SSH through the node running the VM: ssh -J core@<node> cloud-user@<vmi-ip> (node and IP from oc get vmi <vm> -n <ns> -o wide ). If no bastion public key was found and test_vm.ssh_public_key was empty, key login is not possible. Set test_vm.ssh_public_key and recreate the VM. Inside the guest, the data disk is available as /dev/disk/by-id/virtio-datadisk .

docs.text: Removes OpenShift Virtualization, cert-manager, and NFD from the cluster in reverse installation order. Follows the OCP 4.22 uninstall procedure. All VirtualMachine and VirtualMachineInstance objects must be deleted before running — the playbook aborts with a clear message if any remain.

docs.text: HyperConverged CR deleted — virtualization stack deactivated. OpenShift Virtualization Operator, CSV, and CRDs removed. openshift-cnv namespace deleted. cert-manager Operator, CSV, and the cert-manager-operator and cert-manager namespaces deleted. NFD NodeFeatureDiscovery CR, Operator, CSV, and openshift-nfd namespace deleted.
docs.title: Outcomes

docs.text: Requires -e ocp_virt_uninstall_confirm=true — the play aborts immediately without this flag to prevent accidental runs. The variable has no default; setting it in operators.yaml or other vars files is not supported — pass it on the command line. Will abort with a clear message if any VMs or VMIs still exist on the cluster. Cluster operators and compute nodes are not affected. StorageClasses, PVCs, and NFD node labels are not removed by this playbook. operators.yaml must still be present (same requirement as the install playbook).

docs.text: In a text editor of your choice, open the template of the environment variables file . Make a copy of it called all.yaml and paste it into the same directory with its template. all.yaml is your master variables file and you will likely reference it many times throughout the process. The default inventory can be found at inventories/default . The variables marked with an X are required to be filled in. Many values are pre-filled or are optional. Optional values are commented out; in order to use them, remove the # and fill them in. This is the most important step in the process. Take the time to make sure everything here is correct. Note on YAML syntax : Only the lowest value in each hierarchicy needs to be filled in. For example, at the top of the variables file env and z don't need to be filled in, but the cpc_name does. There are X's where input is required to help you with this. Scroll the table to the right to see examples for each variable.

docs.text: Step 3: Set Variables (host_vars) # Overview # Similar to the group_vars file, the host_vars files for each LPAR (KVM host) must be filled in. For each KVM host to be acted upon with Ansible, you must have a corresponding host_vars file named <kvm-hostname>.yaml (i.e. ocpz1.yaml, ocpz2.yaml, ocpz3.yaml), so you must copy and rename the templates found in the host_vars folder accordingly. The variables marked with an X are required to be filled in. Many values are pre-filled or are optional. Optional values are commented out; in order to use them, remove the # and fill them in. Many of the variables in these host_vars files are only required if you are NOT using pre-existing LPARs with RHEL installed. See the Important Note below this first section for more details. This is the most important step in the process. Take the time to make sure everything here is correct. Note on YAML syntax : Only the lowest value in each hierarchicy needs to be filled in. For example, at the top of the variables file networking does not need to be filled in, but the hostname does. There are X's where input is required to help you with this. Scroll the table to the right to see examples for each variable. 1 - KVM Host # Variable Name Description Example networking.hostname The hostname of the LPAR with RHEL installed natively (the KVM host). kvm-host-01 networking.ip The IPv4 address of the LPAR with RHEL installed natively (the KVM host). 192.168.10.2 networking.internal_ip The internal IPv4 address of the LPAR required when booting the LPAR with HiperSocket card. Currently supports only when bastion is on LPAR or on zVM host. Incase of zVM bastion enable the HiperSocket card prior to the playbook run with vmcp commands on the bastion. Alternative Option would be setting up the bridge port on OSA or RoCE. 10.42.6.2 networking.mode Type of network card osa/roce/hipersocket networking.ipv6 IPv6 address for the bastion if use_ipv6 variable is 'True'. fd00::3 networking.subnetmask The subnet that the LPAR resides in within your network. 255.255.255.0 networking.gateway The IPv4 address of the gateway to the network where the KVM host resides. 192.168.10.0 networking.ipv6_gateway IPv6 of he bastion's gateway server. fd00::1 networking.ipv6_prefix IPv6 prefix. 64 networking.nameserver1 The IPv4 address from which the KVM host gets its hostname resolved. 192.168.10.200 networking.nameserver2 (Optional) A second IPv4 address from which the KVM host can get its hostname resolved. Used for high availability. 192.168.10.201 networking.device1 The network interface card from Linux's perspective. Usually enc and then a number that comes from the dev_num of the network adapter. enc100 networking.device2 (Optional) Another Linux network interface card. Usually enc and then a number that comes from the dev_num of the second network adapter. enc1 storage.pool_path The absolute path to a directory on your KVM host that will be used to store qcow2 images for the cluster and other installation artifacts. A sub-directory will be created here that matches your clsuter's metadata name that will act as the cluster's libvirt storage pool directory. Note: all directories present in this path will be made executable for the 'qemu' group, as is required. /home/kvm_admin/VirtualMachines Important Note # You can skip the rest of the variables on this page IF you are using existing LPAR(s) that has RHEL already installed. If you are installing an LPAR based cluster then the information below must be provided and are not optional. You must create a host file corresponding to each lpar node. docs.text: Similar to the group_vars file, the host_vars files for each LPAR (KVM host) must be filled in. For each KVM host to be acted upon with Ansible, you must have a corresponding host_vars file named <kvm-hostname>.yaml (i.e. ocpz1.yaml, ocpz2.yaml, ocpz3.yaml), so you must copy and rename the templates found in the host_vars folder accordingly. The variables marked with an X are required to be filled in. Many values are pre-filled or are optional. Optional values are commented out; in order to use them, remove the # and fill them in. Many of the variables in these host_vars files are only required if you are NOT using pre-existing LPARs with RHEL installed. See the Important Note below this first section for more details. This is the most important step in the process. Take the time to make sure everything here is correct. Note on YAML syntax : Only the lowest value in each hierarchicy needs to be filled in. For example, at the top of the variables file networking does not need to be filled in, but the hostname does. There are X's where input is required to help you with this. Scroll the table to the right to see examples for each variable.

docs.text: Troubleshooting # If you encounter errors while running the main playbook, there are a few things you can do: Double check your variables. Inspect the part that failed by opening the playbook or role at roles/role-name/tasks/main.yaml Google the specific error message. Re-run the role with the verbosity '-v' option to get more debugging information (more v's give more info). For example: ansible-playbook playbooks/setup_bastion.yaml -vvv Use tags To be more selective with what parts of a playbook are run, use tags. To determine what part of a playbook you would like to run, open the playbook you'd like to run and find the roles parameter. Each role has a corresponding tag. There are also occasionally tags for sections of a playbook or within the role themselves. This is especially helpful for troubleshooting. You can add in tags under the name parameter for individual tasks you'd like to run. Here's an example of using a tag: ansible-playbook playbooks/setup_kvm_host.yaml --tags "section_2,section_3" This runs only the parts of the setup_kvm_host playbook marked with tags section_2 and section_3. To use more than one tag, they must be quoted (single or double) and comma-separated (with or without spaces between). E-mail Jacob Emery at jacob.emery@ibm.com If it's a problem with an OpenShift verification step: Open the cockpit to monitor the VMs. In a web browser, go to https://kvm-host-IP-here:9090 Sign-in with your credentials set in the variables file Enable administrative access in the top right. Open the 'Virtual Machines' tab from the left side toolbar. Sometimes it just takes a while, especially if it's lacking resources. Give it some time and then re-reun the playbook/role with tags. If that doesn't work, SSH into the bastion as root ("ssh root@\<bastion-ip-address-here>") and then run, "export KUBECONFIG=/root/ocpinst/auth/kubeconfig" and then "oc whoami" and make sure it ouputs "system:admin". Then run the shell command from the role you would like to check on manually: i.e. 'oc get nodes', 'oc get co', etc. Open the .openshift_install.log file for information on what happened and try to debug the issue.
